chapter: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
title: Who danced and where: tap more popular than jazz
summary: Green says tap was more popular than jazz music, mostly black dancers though whites took it for health, and lists white dancers like Patricola, Barton, Raft and Paul Draper.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: -- entertainment you could have was tap dancing. It was more popular than jazz music. Tap dancing.
Was it mostly whites that were doing it? Or were blacks doing it as well?
You never did have a lot of whites that did tap dancing. They used to take it in schools --
I think they began to discover it, you see?
But they never tried to go along with it and popularize it or anything, see? And they didn't make it a happy medium, as it was. I mean they just would do it, you know, I think for health purposes.
But you were mentioning white performers that were doing it. Eleanor Powell, George M. Cohan.

She was a student. I mean she was a great dancer, but she wasn't no great tap dancer. She was becoming a great tap dancer from Mr. Buddy Bradley. See? I mentioned the great tap dancers in the whites was like Tom Patricola, James Barton, Walter Huston, people like that, men. George Murphy. And George M. Cohan. Even George Primrose, he wasn't no tap dancer, you see? But I mean, that was the most happy medium, it was the most popular. It was more popular than jazz music.
And where was it being performed?
Where in New York? What type of places?

All over. All what they called legitimate, off-Broadway shows. The two a day shows. Like Paul Draper, that's what I meant to say, see? Even George Raft was becoming a dancer. But not in tap dancing, see? He was a visual dancer, George Raft. Something like Sneaky Tucker, but he did jazz. He did a jazz dance to Sweet Georgia Brown, that's what he done, you know.
